title: Ganges water treaty expires in 18 days with no talks scheduled on what replaces it
dek: The 1996 Farakka pact, which governs how much dry-season water reaches Bangladesh and the Hooghly, lapses on 12 December. Dhaka wants a new deal with a guarantee; Delhi says talks belong in the Joint Rivers Commission; Bengal and Bihar want their say.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The treaty that has divided the dry-season flow of the Ganges at Farakka between India and Bangladesh for three decades expires on 12 December, 18 days from now, and the two governments have not scheduled any formal negotiations on renewing or replacing it. The latest meeting of the joint body that monitors the treaty ended in Dhaka on Monday after finalising its annual report, without discussing what comes next, according to members of both delegations.

The stakes are high for West Bengal. The Farakka Barrage in Murshidabad district diverts part of the river into a feeder canal that keeps the Bhagirathi-Hooghly flowing past Kolkata, and how much water stays on the Indian side between January and May is set by the treaty's formula. The state government has asked the Centre not to settle anything that would cut lean-season flows to the Hooghly, the Kolkata port or the erosion-hit districts along the river.

## What happened

The 91st meeting of the Indo-Bangladesh Joint Committee, set up under Article IV of the treaty to record flows at Farakka and at Hardinge Bridge in Bangladesh, opened in Dhaka on Sunday. India's four-member team was led by Sharad Chandra, Commissioner (Farakka) in the Jal Shakti ministry's water resources department; Bangladesh's six-member team by Md Anwar Kadir, a member of the Joint Rivers Commission. The two sides finalised the committee's report on how the treaty worked in 2026.

"This wasn't a meeting on a new treaty. It was a regular meeting of the Joint Rivers Commission," Mr Kadir said, according to reports. Indian officials had described the meeting in advance as a routine exercise to finalise the annual report, reports said.

Bangladesh has been pressing for formal talks since June, when it set up a high-level technical committee and informed New Delhi; in August it asked India to name its negotiating team. On 17 November its water resources minister, Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee, wrote again to his Indian counterpart asking for negotiations to begin before the deadline, reports said. Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, the prime minister's adviser who heads the Bangladeshi committee, said Dhaka "has already completed all necessary preparations related to the treaty".

India's position, as set out repeatedly by the Ministry of External Affairs, is that any discussion should go through existing channels. "We have a Joint Rivers Commission - a structured bilateral mechanism - to deal with issues pertaining to all the rivers," spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at a briefing in June. In February the Minister of State for External Affairs, Kirti Vardhan Singh, told the Lok Sabha that formal renewal talks had not begun, according to reports. Nothing has been announced since.

## What the treaty says

The treaty, signed in New Delhi on 12 December 1996 by Sheikh Hasina and H D Deve Gowda, covers the lean season from 1 January to 31 May, in ten-day blocks. Under its formula, when the flow at Farakka is 70,000 cusecs or less, each country gets half; between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, Bangladesh gets 35,000 and India the rest; above 75,000, India gets 40,000 and Bangladesh the rest. From 11 March to 10 May, the driest weeks, each side is guaranteed 35,000 cusecs in alternate ten-day periods.

Based on 1949-88 averages, its schedule expects flows to fall from about 1,07,500 cusecs in early January to about 61,000 in late April. If the flow falls below 50,000 cusecs in any ten-day period, Article II says the two governments "will enter into immediate consultations to make adjustments on an emergency basis". There is no guaranteed minimum for Bangladesh below that level, which is the gap Dhaka now wants closed. Article XII is short: the treaty "shall remain in force for a period of thirty years and it shall be renewable on the basis of mutual consent". It says nothing about what happens if there is no agreement.

## Background

The treaty ended two decades of dispute that began when India commissioned the Farakka Barrage in 1975. A 1977 agreement included a guarantee that Bangladesh would receive at least 80 per cent of its share in a crisis; it lapsed in 1982 and was followed by short memorandums before the 1996 pact. "Our main priority will be to bring back the guarantee clause that was included in the 1977 agreement," Mr Anee said in September, according to reports. Dhaka wants a new treaty, not a simple extension.

The politics have changed on both sides. Sheikh Hasina, who signed the treaty for Bangladesh, has lived in India since she was ousted in August 2024; she has now named 16 December, four days after the treaty lapses, for a return to Dhaka that the government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman says will end in her arrest. Relations between Delhi and the BNP government, in office since February, remain cool, and the Bangladeshi prime minister has not visited India.

Within India, water is a state subject, and two states want to be heard. Bihar has opposed renewing the treaty in its present form, arguing that it limits water for drinking, irrigation and industry upstream; the JD(U) Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Kumar Jha has called for it to be ended, and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar told Bihar in September that its interests would be considered, reports said. A parliamentary committee report said the Jal Shakti ministry set up an inter-ministerial committee in July 2023, with representatives of West Bengal and Bihar, to review the treaty.

West Bengal submitted a proposal to that committee in August asking that the lean-season flow through the Bhagirathi-Hooghly be protected, that erosion in Malda, Murshidabad and Nadia be addressed in any new deal, and that "no conclusions be finalised" without administrative-level talks first, according to reports quoting state officials. Bengal has a history here: the Teesta water-sharing agreement was ready for signing in 2011 but was dropped after the then chief minister, Mamata Banerjee, objected.

## What they are saying

Syeda Rizwana Hasan, a former water resources adviser in Dhaka, warned that "geopolitics" may dictate the treaty's future and urged Bangladesh to keep the talks separate from wider tensions with India. On the Indian side, the ministry spokesperson said on 20 November that India wants a constructive relationship with Bangladesh while protecting its own interests, reports said. Neither government has said whether it would accept a short extension of the current terms while a new treaty is negotiated.

## What happens next

The treaty lapses at the end of 12 December. The next lean season, the period it actually governs, begins on 1 January. Experts on both sides note that expiry does not mean India will stop releasing water at Farakka, but without a treaty there would be no agreed formula and no binding guarantee during the driest weeks, which is Bangladesh's main fear. Any new deal or interim arrangement would need a political decision in Delhi after consultation with Kolkata and Patna, and a meeting at the level of ministers, none of which is yet on the calendar.

## Timeline

- 1977: First sharing agreement, with a guarantee clause; lapses in 1982
- 12 Dec 1996: Hasina and Deve Gowda sign the 30-year treaty
- Jul 2023: Jal Shakti ministry forms a review committee including Bengal and Bihar
- Jun 2026: Bangladesh forms a technical committee and seeks talks
- 17 Nov 2026: Dhaka's water minister writes to Delhi again
- 22-23 Nov 2026: Joint Committee meets in Dhaka; renewal not discussed
- 12 Dec 2026: Treaty expires
- 1 Jan 2027: Lean season begins

image.alt: Stacked bar chart of the 1996 Ganges treaty's indicative sharing schedule at Farakka for each ten-day period from January to May, based on 1949-88 average flows. Average flow falls from 107,516 cusecs in 1-10 January (India 40,000, Bangladesh 67,516) to 60,992 cusecs in 21-30 April (India 25,992, Bangladesh 35,000), then rises to 81,854 cusecs in 21-31 May (India 40,000, Bangladesh 41,854). Between 11 March and 10 May each side is guaranteed 35,000 cusecs in alternate ten-day periods.
image.caption: The treaty's schedule: shares tighten to about 35,000 cusecs each in the driest weeks of March and April.
